\subsection{Multislice 4D-STEM simulation}
\label{sec:sim}

\paragraph{Overview: the forward operator.}
The simulation is the forward model $\mathcal{S}$ that maps a known atomic structure to the
data a microscope would record,
\begin{equation}
  \mathbf{I} \;=\; \mathcal{S}\big(\{\mathbf{r}_a, Z_a\}\big) \;+\; \text{noise},
  \label{eq:fwd}
\end{equation}
with $\{\mathbf{r}_a,Z_a\}$ the atomic positions and species. It composes three stages ---
coherent multislice propagation, an incoherent average over thermal displacements, and a
photon-counting model --- set out in turn below and sketched in Fig.~\ref{fig:acq}. We state
$\mathcal{S}$ explicitly because the reconstruction of Sec.~\ref{sec:recon} inverts the
\emph{same} operator, and the point-spread function used for localisation
(Sec.~\ref{sec:atomfind}) is the response of the composed forward--inverse pair to a single
atom; the biases and the null space introduced here reappear there as structured
uncertainty.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figs/acquisition}
  \caption{Multislice 4D-STEM acquisition: the composed forward operator $\mathcal{S}$ of
    Eq.~\eqref{eq:fwd}.}
  \label{fig:acq}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Coherent multislice.}
At $300$\,keV the (relativistic) electron wavelength is
\begin{equation}
  \lambda \;=\; \frac{h}{\sqrt{2m_0 eU\big(1+\tfrac{eU}{2m_0c^2}\big)}}
  \;=\; 1.969\times10^{-2}\,\text{\AA},
  \label{eq:wavelength}
\end{equation}
for accelerating voltage $U$. The convergent probe is the aperture-limited, aberrated point
source
\begin{equation}
  \psi_{\mathrm{p}}(\mathbf{r};\mathbf{r}_p)
  \;=\; \mathcal{F}^{-1}\!\big\{A(\mathbf{k})\,e^{-i\chi(\mathbf{k})}\big\}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_p),
  \qquad \chi(\mathbf{k}) = \pi\lambda\,\Delta f\,\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert^2,
  \label{eq:probe}
\end{equation}
where $A$ is the objective aperture ($A=1$ for $\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert<\alpha/\lambda$, else
$0$), $\alpha=100$\,mrad the convergence semi-angle, and the aberration function $\chi$ is
kept to the defocus term only (the instrument is aberration-corrected), with $\Delta
f=-20$\,\AA{} a $20$\,\AA{} overfocus. The wave is propagated through the specimen by the
multislice recursion \citep{CowleyMoodie1957,Kirkland2010},
\begin{equation}
  \psi_{n+1} \;=\; \mathcal{P}_{\Delta z}\!\otimes\!\big[\,t_n(\mathbf{r})\,\psi_n(\mathbf{r})\,\big],
  \qquad
  t_n(\mathbf{r}) = \exp\!\big[\,i\,\sigma\, v_n(\mathbf{r})\,\big],
  \label{eq:multislice}
\end{equation}
in which each slice imprints a phase through its projected potential
$v_n(\mathbf{r})=\int_{z_n}^{z_n+\Delta z}V(\mathbf{r},z)\,\mathrm{d}z$ with interaction
constant $\sigma=2\pi m e\lambda/h^2$, and $\mathcal{P}_{\Delta z}$ is the Fresnel propagator,
acting as multiplication by $\tilde{P}(\mathbf{k})=\exp(-i\pi\lambda\Delta z\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert^2)$
in Fourier space. The recorded quantity is the far-field intensity of the exit wave,
\begin{equation}
  I(\mathbf{r}_p,\mathbf{k}) \;=\; \big\lvert\,\Psi_{\mathrm{exit}}(\mathbf{k};\mathbf{r}_p)\,\big\rvert^2,
  \qquad \Psi_{\mathrm{exit}}=\mathcal{F}\psi_N .
  \label{eq:intensity}
\end{equation}
We use the GPU implementation in abTEM \citep{MadsenSusi2021}; projected potentials follow
the constrained parameterisation of \citet{LobatoVanDyck2014}, evaluated at $\Delta z=2$\,\AA{}
(reduced to $0.5$\,\AA{} for the finely sampled reconstructions, well below the thickness at
which the split-step approximation of Eq.~\eqref{eq:multislice} biases high-angle intensity).
The specimen is a PbTiO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ ferroelectric labyrinth supercell
($70.0\times70.0\times47.9$\,\AA), oriented with the beam along a $\langle100\rangle$ axis and
padded to a square $70$\,\AA{} field, giving $\approx70$\,\AA{} of material along the beam; the
box is retained uncropped so the laterally broadening exit wave does not alias at the periodic
boundaries. The probe is scanned over a $20$\,\AA{} window at $0.10$--$0.15$\,\AA{} steps, so
that adjacent illuminations overlap by ${>}90\%$ --- the redundancy that makes the inverse
problem of Sec.~\ref{sec:recon} well-posed \citep{Ophus2019,RodenburgFaulkner2004}.

\paragraph{Thermal diffuse scattering.}
Atoms are not stationary, and the elastic model of Eq.~\eqref{eq:multislice} alone would
overstate the coherent signal. Thermal motion is included in the frozen-phonon approximation
\citep{LoaneXuSilcox1991}, valid because the electron transit time ($\sim\!10^{-16}$\,s) is
far shorter than a phonon period ($\sim\!10^{-12}$\,s): each electron sees a static, randomly
displaced lattice, and the measurement is the incoherent average of the intensity over the
displacement ensemble,
\begin{equation}
  I(\mathbf{k}) \;=\; \big\langle\,\lvert\Psi(\mathbf{k})\rvert^2\,\big\rangle_{\mathbf{u}}
  \;\approx\; \frac{1}{N_\mathrm{ph}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_\mathrm{ph}}\big\lvert\Psi_j(\mathbf{k})\big\rvert^2,
  \qquad N_\mathrm{ph}=16,
  \label{eq:fp}
\end{equation}
each configuration $j$ displacing every atom by an independent Gaussian draw $\mathbf{u}$. The
consequence is quantified by the Debye--Waller factor: for isotropic Gaussian displacements
with one-dimensional variance $\langle u^2\rangle$ and momentum transfer $\mathbf{q}$
($\lvert\mathbf{q}\rvert=4\pi\sin\theta/\lambda$), the ensemble-averaged single-atom amplitude
carries
\begin{equation}
  \big\langle e^{\,i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{u}}\big\rangle
  \;=\; e^{-M}, \qquad
  M \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\lvert\mathbf{q}\rvert^2\langle u^2\rangle \;=\; B\,s^2,
  \quad s=\tfrac{\sin\theta}{\lambda},\; B=8\pi^2\langle u^2\rangle .
  \label{eq:dw}
\end{equation}
The coherent intensity is thus attenuated by $e^{-2M}$, most strongly at high angle (high
$s$), and the removed intensity re-emerges as a diffuse background (Fig.~\ref{fig:dw}). Because
$M\propto B$, this attenuation is species-dependent, so we set displacement amplitudes
\emph{per species} from tabulated room-temperature isotropic $B$ \citep{Peng1996} --- passing
the three-dimensional magnitude $\sigma=\sqrt{3B/8\pi^2}$ (as $\langle u^2\rangle=B/8\pi^2$ per
axis) --- rather than one value for all. The A-site lead and the oxygen vibrate roughly twice
as far as titanium ($B_\mathrm{Pb}=0.90$, $B_\mathrm{O}=0.80$, $B_\mathrm{Sr}=0.55$,
$B_\mathrm{Ti}=0.45$\,\AA$^2$); a single averaged displacement would misweight the diffuse
background of exactly the light species the localisation stage most struggles to detect. The
convergence of Eq.~\eqref{eq:fp} in $N_\mathrm{ph}$ was checked against a doubled
configuration count.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.62\linewidth]{figs/debye_waller}
  \caption{Debye--Waller attenuation of the coherent signal and the compensating thermal
    diffuse background produced by the frozen-phonon average, Eq.~\eqref{eq:fp}.}
  \label{fig:dw}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Detection and dose.}
The full $\approx200$\,mrad diffraction plane is recorded and binned $4\times4$ to
$356\times356$ pixels, keeping the zero-order disc centred so the reciprocal-space calibration
the reconstruction depends on is exact. abTEM flux-normalises each pattern to
$\tilde I$ ($\sum_{\mathbf{k}}\tilde I=1$); a finite electron budget is imposed as the last
stage of $\mathcal{S}$ by a shot-noise model,
\begin{equation}
  n(\mathbf{r}_p,\mathbf{k}) \;\sim\; \mathrm{Poisson}\!\big(N_e\,\tilde I(\mathbf{r}_p,\mathbf{k})\big),
  \qquad N_e = D\,s^2 ,
  \label{eq:poisson}
\end{equation}
with $D$ the dose (e\,\AA$^{-2}$) and $s$ the scan step, so $N_e$ is the electrons incident
per pattern. Equation~\eqref{eq:poisson} is exactly the likelihood the reconstruction is
matched to (Sec.~\ref{sec:recon}) and that ultimately sets the statistical component of the
localisation uncertainty. Doses of $10^{4}$--$10^{10}$\,e\,\AA$^{-2}$ are used: the coherent,
high-fluence limit gives the near-noiseless reference, the thermally-averaged
counting-limited data the realistic test.

\subsection{Multislice electron ptychography}
\label{sec:recon}

\paragraph{The inverse problem.}
Reconstruction inverts $\mathcal{S}$: from the recorded patterns it estimates the complex
specimen transmission by iterative ptychography \citep{RodenburgFaulkner2004,Wakonig2020},
which exploits the scan redundancy and has reached deep sub-\aa{}ngstr\"om lateral resolution
for electrons \citep{Jiang2018}. To resolve structure \emph{along} the beam the single
multiplicative projection is replaced by a multislice object \citep{MaidenHumphryRodenburg2012}:
the specimen is modelled as a stack of $N_L$ transmission slices
$q_l(\mathbf{r})=\exp[i\sigma v_l(\mathbf{r})]$, and for a probe at scan position
$\mathbf{r}_j$ the model exit wave is the \emph{same} multislice operator $\mathcal{M}$ as in
Eq.~\eqref{eq:multislice} applied through the estimated slices,
\begin{equation}
  \psi_j \;=\; \mathcal{M}\big[\{q_l\},\,P(\cdot-\mathbf{r}_j)\big],
  \qquad
  I_j^{\mathrm{model}}(\mathbf{k}) \;=\; \big\lvert\mathcal{F}\psi_j(\mathbf{k})\big\rvert^2,
  \label{eq:ptycho_fwd}
\end{equation}
with $P$ the probe. The unknowns are the object stack $\{q_l\}$ (hence $\{v_l\}$) and the
probe; jointly recovering the slices is what turns a single-orientation measurement into a
depth-resolved, optically sectioned reconstruction without a tilt series
\citep{Gao2017,Chen2021} (Fig.~\ref{fig:ptycho}). We reconstruct $N_L=70$ (coherent) or $105$
(thermally-averaged) slices across the $\approx70$\,\AA{} thickness, i.e.\ depth sampling
$\Delta z_\mathrm{rec}\approx1.0$ and $0.67$\,\AA, with the hollow-detector inner angle set to
zero so the full recorded cone constrains the object.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figs/ptycho_inverse}
  \caption{Multislice ptychography as inversion of $\mathcal{S}$: joint least-squares
    maximum-likelihood recovery of the object slices and the probe.}
  \label{fig:ptycho}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Maximum-likelihood estimation.}
The estimate is the minimiser of a data-fidelity term that is the negative log-likelihood of
the noise model of Eq.~\eqref{eq:poisson}. PtychoShelves \citep{Wakonig2020} uses the
least-squares maximum-likelihood (LSQ-ML) engine of \citet{Odstrcil2018}, which in the
shot-noise regime reduces to the variance-stabilised amplitude metric
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal{D}(\Theta) \;=\; \sum_{j}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}
  \Big(\sqrt{I_j^{\mathrm{model}}(\mathbf{k};\Theta)} - \sqrt{I_j^{\mathrm{meas}}(\mathbf{k})}\Big)^{2},
  \qquad \Theta=\big(\{q_l\},\{P_m\}\big),
  \label{eq:datafidelity}
\end{equation}
the Anscombe-type surrogate for the exact Poisson log-likelihood
$\sum(I^{\mathrm{model}}-I^{\mathrm{meas}}\log I^{\mathrm{model}})$
\citep{ThibaultGuizar2012}. The reconstruction is thus a maximum-a-posteriori estimate
$\hat\Theta=\arg\min_\Theta\,\mathcal{D}(\Theta)+\mathcal{R}(\Theta)$ with $\mathcal{R}$ a
regulariser; \emph{we set $\mathcal{R}=0$ on the inter-layer (depth) coupling}, so the axial
structure is determined by the data rather than by a smoothness prior. This is a deliberate
choice: a depth prior would bias exactly the axial coordinate whose uncertainty we later
quantify, at the price of a noisier deep reconstruction, which we characterise directly rather
than suppress. Optimisation uses a two-stage schedule --- a down-sampled $178$-pixel pre-solve
to fix the low-frequency object and probe, then a full-resolution $356$-pixel refinement ---
which accelerates convergence and reduces stagnation in poor local minima of the non-convex
$\mathcal{D}$.

\paragraph{Partial coherence and the probe.}
For the coherent reference a single fixed probe is used. For the thermally-averaged,
counting-limited data the illumination is described by a mixed state --- an incoherent sum of
mutually orthogonal probe modes $\{P_m\}$ \citep{ThibaultMenzel2013} ---
\begin{equation}
  I_j(\mathbf{k}) \;=\; \sum_{m}\big\lvert\mathcal{F}\,\mathcal{M}\big[\{q_l\},P_m(\cdot-\mathbf{r}_j)\big](\mathbf{k})\big\rvert^2,
  \qquad \rho=\sum_m \lvert P_m\rangle\langle P_m\rvert,
  \label{eq:mixed}
\end{equation}
equivalently a low-rank coherence (density) operator $\rho$, with the modes released after a
single-mode burn-in. These extra incoherent degrees of freedom absorb the thermal diffuse
background of Eq.~\eqref{eq:fp} and any residual partial coherence, which a single coherent
mode would otherwise be forced to explain by corrupting the object $\{q_l\}$ itself
\citep{ThibaultMenzel2013}; slow probe variation across the scan, where present, is further
accommodated by orthogonal probe relaxation \citep{Odstrcil2016}. In estimation terms the
modes are nuisance latent variables that make the object estimate robust to model
mis-specification of the coherence.

\paragraph{Depth resolution and the missing cone.}
The anisotropy that dominates the localisation problem is a property of the operator
$\mathcal{S}$, not of the noise. In the weak-phase linearisation a single-orientation
measurement transfers an object spatial frequency $\mathbf{K}=(\mathbf{K}_\parallel,K_z)$ only
where the Ewald-sphere cap, swept over the aperture of semi-angle $\alpha$, has support; the
accessible axial band at low lateral frequency is
\begin{equation}
  \lvert K_z\rvert \;\lesssim\; \frac{\alpha^2}{2\lambda},
  \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
  \delta x \approx \frac{\lambda}{2\alpha}\approx 0.10\,\text{\AA},
  \quad
  \delta z \approx \frac{\lambda}{\alpha^2}\approx 2.0\,\text{\AA}.
  \label{eq:missingcone}
\end{equation}
Frequencies in the double cone about the $K_z$ axis are never measured --- the null space of
$\mathcal{S}$ --- so the reconstructed response of a single atom is strongly anisotropic:
tight in-plane, elongated along the beam by the ratio $\delta z/\delta x\approx 2\alpha\approx
20$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:cone}). This is the same missing-cone, limited-angle regime familiar from
limited-angle tomography, reached here by multislice ptychography rather than by tilting
\citep{Chen2021}. Crucially for what follows, the elongation is a \emph{deterministic,
correlated} uncertainty in the axial coordinate --- not statistical scatter --- so it neither
averages away with dose nor is captured by a residual-based error estimate; the reconstructed
single-atom response is measured directly and used as the three-dimensional point-spread
function of the localisation model in Sec.~\ref{sec:atomfind}, which must propagate this
correlation explicitly.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figs/missing_cone}
  \caption{The single-orientation missing cone (null space of the forward operator) and the
    anisotropic three-dimensional point-spread function it produces.}
  \label{fig:cone}
\end{figure}
